title: Lineage and a Certificate
bigQuestion: When two schools both claim to teach the true art, what makes a rank certificate count, and who decides?

story.title: Two Grandfathers on One Wall
story.kicker: Two framed certificates hang side by side, and each traces its art to a different teacher.
paragraphs: Picture a small school in a strip mall. Two framed certificates hang behind the front desk. One carries the seal of a large national federation and a registration number. The other is signed by a teacher who says his own teacher learned from the art's founder. Each paper names a different grandfather, the teacher two steps back in the line.

Both papers make a claim about *authority*, the right to teach and to promote students. In older Japanese schools that right passed on handwritten scrolls from one teacher to one student. In the twentieth century, federations began to print numbered certificates and keep lists of every holder.

The arguments over those papers are part of the history of the arts. When Funakoshi Gichin died in 1957, his students split into rival groups. When the Gracie family carried its jiu-jitsu from Brazil to California, cousins argued over the family name in a United States court. Each dispute asked who owns an art once its founder is gone.

This chapter follows the paper trail: scrolls in old Japanese schools, titles from a Kyoto association founded in 1895, a Tokyo hall destroyed in 1945, a trademark case decided in 2000 and the federations that register ranks today.
story.think: If a certificate is only paper, why do people frame it? What would make you trust one certificate more than another?

lessons.title: Licenses in the Old Schools
lessons.mainIdea: Before belts, Japanese martial schools passed teaching authority on handwritten scrolls given by one teacher to chosen students.
reading: Japan had hundreds of martial schools, each called a *ryūha*, long before judo or karate had ranks. Tenshin Shōden Katori Shintō-ryū, a school of swordsmanship from the 1400s, is often named among the oldest that still teaches. Schools like it kept their teaching inside a line of teachers, and outsiders rarely saw it.

A student in such a school received paper licenses at a few turning points. An early scroll might list the school's lessons by name, and it was called a mokuroku, meaning catalog. The highest level was often a *menkyo kaiden*, a license of full transmission. It said the holder had received the whole school and could pass it on.

These licenses were few, and there was no public list of them. A teacher might give a full license to only a handful of students in a lifetime. Authority rested on a personal tie between two people, not on an office. That older pattern still shapes how many schools talk about a teacher's line today.

words.d: a Japanese school or lineage of a martial art, passed from teacher to student
a license of full transmission in an old Japanese school, showing the holder received all of it
the accepted right to teach, judge or promote others
the line of teachers and students through which an art has been passed down

The first colored belt in judo

choices: A Japanese school or lineage of a martial art

choices: A public office listed every license holder

check.why: Few licenses were given, with no public list, so authority came from the teacher who signed.

lessons.title: Titles From Kyoto, 1895
lessons.mainIdea: The Dai Nippon Butoku Kai, founded in Kyoto in 1895, gave Japan's martial arts a national body that granted teaching titles.
reading: In 1895 the *Dai Nippon Butoku Kai*, the Greater Japan Martial Virtue Society, was founded in Kyoto. It had close ties to the government and the imperial household. In 1899 it opened the Butokuden, a large practice hall near Heian Shrine. It held yearly demonstrations there that drew teachers from many schools.

In the early 1900s the society began to grant *teaching titles*, including hanshi and kyōshi, to senior teachers. A title from a national society meant something different from a scroll signed by one teacher. It told the public that a central body had approved the holder. Judo, kendo and later karate teachers sought these titles.

The society grew into a state organization during the war years. After Japan's defeat, the Allied occupation dissolved it in 1946, along with other groups tied to the wartime state. New federations for judo, kendo and karate took over the work of grading. The idea of a central body that approves teachers outlived the society itself.

words.d: the Greater Japan Martial Virtue Society, founded in Kyoto in 1895
an honor such as hanshi or kyōshi given to a senior teacher by a national body
control of a country by foreign armed forces, as Allied forces controlled Japan from 1945 to 1952

look.title: Two Kinds of Approval
look.text: In 1890 a sword teacher's standing depended on the scrolls his own teacher gave him. By 1910 he could also hold a title granted by a society in Kyoto that had ties to the government.
look.prompt: What changed about who could approve a teacher? Who gained power from that change?

check.q: Where and when was the Dai Nippon Butoku Kai founded?
check.why: The society was founded in Kyoto in 1895.

check.q: What did the society's teaching titles tell the public?
choices: That a central body had approved the teacher
That the teacher had won an Olympic medal
That the teacher owned a trademark
That the teacher had no lineage
check.why: A title such as hanshi showed approval from a national society, not only from one teacher.

check.q: What happened to the society in 1946?
check.why: Occupation authorities dissolved it with other groups tied to the wartime state.

lessons.title: Karate Takes Dan Ranks
lessons.mainIdea: Karate borrowed numbered dan ranks from judo in the 1920s, which let schools on the mainland show rank in a way outsiders understood.
reading: Kanō Jigorō gave the first judo *dan* ranks in 1883. Dan means step or grade, and each black-belt level had a number. The system let judo schools across Japan speak one language of rank. Other arts watched it work in schools, universities and the police.

Karate came to mainland Japan from Okinawa in the early 1920s. In Okinawa, teachers had passed on the art without belts or printed grades. In 1924 Funakoshi Gichin awarded the first karate dan ranks to some of his students in Tokyo. Karate teachers also adopted a jacket and belt close to judo's.

Numbered ranks made karate easier to fit into Japanese universities and into the Butoku Kai. They also changed the question of authority. A student's rank now depended on who signed the certificate and which group the signer belonged to. When groups later split, their certificates split too.

words.d: a numbered black-belt grade, first used in judo by Kanō Jigorō in 1883
a signed paper that records a rank or license
the main island of the Ryukyu Islands, where karate took shape before it reached mainland Japan

check.why: Funakoshi awarded the first karate dan ranks in Tokyo in 1924.

check.q: How did numbered ranks change the question of authority in karate?

check.why: A certificate carries the authority of its signer and group, so splits between groups divided ranks too.

sections.title: A Founder Dies, a Name Divides

lessons.title: A Pen Name Becomes a Style
lessons.mainIdea: Shōtōkan began as the name of Funakoshi's Tokyo hall, taken from his pen name, and later became the name of a style.
reading: Funakoshi Gichin wrote poetry under the *pen name* Shōtō, often translated as pine waves. In 1939 his students opened a practice hall in Tokyo. They named it Shōtōkan, meaning Shōtō's hall. Funakoshi himself mostly called what he taught simply karate-dō.

The hall burned in American air raids on Tokyo in 1945. The building was gone, but its name stayed. Students and later groups used Shōtōkan as the name of a *style*, one branch of karate with its own teachers and forms. Other branches took names in a similar way, from a teacher, a phrase or a place.

Gōjū-ryū is one example. Miyagi Chōjun of Naha, Okinawa, chose the name, meaning hard-soft school, from a line in an old Chinese text on fighting arts. It was registered with the Butoku Kai in the early 1930s. A style name gave a group a label that could be written on a certificate and a sign.

words.d: a name a writer uses in place of a real name
one named branch of an art, with its own line of teachers
'Shōtō's hall,' Funakoshi's Tokyo hall of 1939, later the name of a karate style

look.title: A Hall and a Label
look.text: A building opens in Tokyo in 1939 with a name carved over the door. Six years later the building is gone. Decades later, schools on several continents print that same name on their signs.
look.prompt: What did the name carry that the building could not? Why might many groups want to use it?

lessons.title: The Association Splits
lessons.mainIdea: After founders die, rival groups often claim the same name, and some of those claims end up in court.
reading: The *Japan Karate Association*, or JKA, was founded in Tokyo in 1949. Funakoshi was honored as its chief instructor. Nakayama Masatoshi led its teaching for decades and sent instructors abroad in the 1950s and 1960s. Some of Funakoshi's older students formed a separate group, the Shōtōkai, and did not join.

Funakoshi died in 1957, and Nakayama died in 1987. In 1990 the JKA split into rival groups, each saying it was the true association. The dispute over which group could use the JKA name went to the courts in Japan. Instructors around the world had to choose a side, and their students' certificates followed them.

The JKA story shows a common pattern called a *schism*, a split in a group over who holds authority. Similar splits happened in many karate, taekwondo and kung fu groups. Each new group usually kept the founder's photograph on the wall. The fight was not over the past but over who speaks for it now.

words.d: a karate body founded in Tokyo in 1949, often called the JKA
a split in a group over who holds authority
a group or person competing with another for the same thing

look.title: Which Group Is the Real One?
look.text: Two groups use the same name. One kept the office and the records. The other kept most of the senior instructors. Both hang the founder's photograph and both issue certificates in his art's name.
look.prompt: What evidence would each group point to? Why might a court, not a teacher, end up deciding who may use the name?

check.q: When was the Japan Karate Association founded?
check.why: The JKA was founded in Tokyo in 1949.

check.q: What is a schism?
choices: A split in a group over who holds authority
A hall named after a teacher
check.why: A schism is a split, like the JKA's in 1990.

check.q: What happened to students' certificates when instructors chose sides after 1990?
choices: They were all cancelled by law

check.why: A certificate carries the authority of a group, so it went with the instructor's choice.

lessons.title: A Number on the Paper
lessons.mainIdea: Large bodies such as the Kodokan and the Kukkiwon made rank checkable by giving each certificate a number in a central register.
reading: The Kodokan in Tokyo, the school Kanō founded in 1882, has kept records of the judo ranks it awards since its early years. A Kodokan rank can be checked against its books. National judo bodies in many countries also keep their own *registers* of promotions. The International Judo Federation sets the rules for rank used in its world events.

Taekwondo built a similar system later. The Kukkiwon in Seoul issues dan certificates with a registration number to students in many countries. A teacher abroad can apply for a student's Kukkiwon rank through the proper channels. The number lets anyone ask whether a certificate is real.

A register changes what a certificate means. Under the old scroll system, trust came from knowing the teacher. Under a register, trust comes from an office that can answer a question. Critics say registers can turn rank into a fee; supporters say they protect students from false claims. Both sides are describing the same *bureaucracy*, an office that runs by records and rules.

words.d: an official list, such as a list of every rank a body has granted
an office or system that works through written records and fixed rules
the judo school Kanō Jigorō founded in Tokyo in 1882

look.title: Checking a Rank
look.text: A parent sees two black-belt certificates. One has a registration number from a national body and a phone number for its office. The other has a signature and a gold seal but no number.
look.prompt: What can the parent check for each one? What might the second certificate still prove, even without a number?

check.q: What does a registration number on a certificate allow?
choices: It makes the holder an Olympian
It replaces the teacher's signature by law
It proves the art is the oldest
It lets someone ask a central office whether the rank is real
check.why: A number ties the paper to a register that can be checked.

check.q: What is a bureaucracy?
choices: An office that works through records and rules

check.why: A bureaucracy, like a rank register, runs on records and fixed rules.

check.q: Which body issues numbered taekwondo dan certificates from Seoul?
check.why: The Kukkiwon in Seoul issues dan certificates with registration numbers.

lessons.title: Maeda Settles in Belém
lessons.mainIdea: A Kodokan judo teacher, Maeda Mitsuyo, settled in Brazil and taught the Gracie brothers, starting a lineage that later took their family name.
reading: Maeda Mitsuyo trained at the Kodokan in Tokyo and left Japan in 1904. For about ten years he toured the United States, Europe, Cuba and Mexico, taking on challengers. In Brazil he was often called Conde Koma. He arrived in Brazil in 1914 and settled in Belém, a port city at the mouth of the Amazon.

In Belém, Maeda taught several local students. Carlos Gracie, born in 1902 to a family of Scottish descent, was one of them. Carlos later taught his younger brothers, including Hélio Gracie. The brothers opened an academy in Rio de Janeiro in the 1920s. At the time, many Brazilians still called the art jiu-jitsu, an older word for Japanese grappling schools.

Over the next decades the Gracies built a public name through challenge matches and newspaper coverage. Their version became known as *Brazilian jiu-jitsu*. The family name and the art's name grew so close that many people treated them as one. That closeness would later become a legal question.

words.d: the grappling art that grew in Brazil from Maeda's teaching, closely tied to the Gracie family
an older spelling of jūjutsu, the name for many Japanese grappling schools
a public contest in which a teacher invites outsiders to test the school

look.title: Dates in a Brazilian Lineage
rows: Rorion Gracie moves to the U.S.

look.prompt: Which came first, the family's move to the United States or the first federation? What might that order mean for who held authority?

lessons.title: Other Lines From Maeda
lessons.mainIdea: Maeda taught more than one family, and other Brazilian lineages that do not carry the Gracie name also trace back to him.
reading: Maeda's students in Belém were not only Gracies. Luiz França also learned from him and later taught in Rio de Janeiro. França's student Oswaldo Fadda opened his own academy in a working-class area of Rio's north zone. Fadda's students entered competitions under their own name, not the Gracie name.

Historians of the art point to these lines to show that lineage is a tree, not a single trunk. A tree has *branches*, separate lines that start from one teacher and grow apart. Some Brazilian schools stress the Fadda line on their walls. Others trace to Maeda through the Gracies, and some trace through both.

The story of the Fadda line also shows class in Brazilian history. The Gracie academy drew many students from wealthier parts of Rio. Fadda taught in poorer neighborhoods and at low cost. When a school hangs a *family tree* chart, it is choosing which branch of this history to honor.

words.d: a separate line of teachers that starts from a shared teacher and grows apart
a chart that shows a school's line of teachers back to a founder
a Brazilian jiu-jitsu teacher in Rio de Janeiro whose line runs back to Maeda through Luiz França

look.title: Two Charts, One Root
look.text: School A's wall chart runs Maeda, then Carlos Gracie, then Hélio Gracie. School B's chart runs Maeda, then Luiz França, then Oswaldo Fadda. Both charts are drawn in the same style and both end with today's teacher.
look.prompt: Can both charts be accurate? What would you look for to test each one?

check.why: Fadda learned from Luiz França, who learned from Maeda.

lessons.title: A Family Name in Court
lessons.mainIdea: When the Gracie name became a U.S. trademark, members of the same family argued in federal court over who could use it.
reading: Rorion Gracie, a son of Hélio, moved to southern California in 1978. He taught in his garage and later opened an academy in Torrance. In November 1993 he helped start the Ultimate Fighting Championship, whose first event was held in Denver. His brother Royce won that event, and the family name spread quickly.

Rorion registered Gracie Jiu-Jitsu as a *trademark* in the United States. A trademark is a word or symbol that tells buyers who is selling a product or service. His cousin Carley Gracie, who also taught in California, challenged the mark. The dispute went to trial and reached the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, which ruled in 2000.

The case showed how a family name, a *brand* and an art can pull apart. Some relatives wanted the name to stay open to anyone in the family line. Others wanted a single owner who could control quality. Courts answered only the legal question of the mark. They did not decide who teaches the art best.

words.d: a word or symbol, protected by law, that tells buyers who is selling a product or service
a name used to sell something and to tell it apart from others
a higher court that reviews the decision of a trial court

lessons.title: A Federation Registers Belts
lessons.mainIdea: Brazilian jiu-jitsu federations founded in 1994 and 2002 added a register and tournament rules to an art once run by families and academies.
reading: In 1994 Carlos Gracie Jr., a son of Carlos Gracie, led the founding of the Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Confederation in Rio de Janeiro. Its world championship began in 1996. In 2002 the International Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Federation, or IBJJF, was founded to run events outside Brazil. A *federation* is a body that joins many clubs under shared rules.

The IBJJF keeps a register of black belts and sets minimum ages and years at belt levels for its events. To enter an IBJJF event, an athlete's rank must follow those rules. Teachers who belong can check a rival school's claim against the list. Not every school joins, and other bodies run their own events and registers.

A federation's power comes from *membership*, not from law. A school that never joins can still teach and give belts. But its students cannot enter that federation's events with those ranks until they meet its rules. Tournaments, rather than scrolls, became one of the main places where rank claims were tested in public.

words.d: a body that joins many clubs or schools under shared rules
belonging to a group and agreeing to follow its rules
the International Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Federation, founded in 2002

look.title: What an International Federation Does
look.text: The Olympic Charter describes international federations as bodies that administer their sports at the world level. National federations inside each country follow the international federation's rules for their sport.
look.prompt: Brazilian jiu-jitsu is not an Olympic sport. Why might its federation still copy this model of world and national bodies?

check.q: Who led the founding of the Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Confederation in 1994?
check.why: Carlos Gracie Jr., a son of Carlos Gracie, led its founding in 1994.

check.q: Where does a federation's power over rank come from?
check.why: A school that never joins can still teach; a federation controls only its own events and lists.

check.q: When was the IBJJF founded?
check.why: The International Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Federation was founded in 2002.

lessons.title: What the Law Protects
lessons.mainIdea: United States trademark law can protect a school's brand, but it cannot make one group the owner of a whole art's ordinary name.
reading: The *Lanham Act* of 1946 is the main federal trademark law in the United States. It lets a business register a mark with the Patent and Trademark Office. A registered mark can stop rivals from using a confusingly similar name to sell the same kind of service. Martial arts schools and associations have registered names, logos and patches under it.

The law also has a limit. A *generic* word, the ordinary name for a whole kind of thing, cannot be anyone's trademark. Words like karate or judo name whole arts, so no one can own them for teaching. A school can own a special name built around a generic word, such as a logo or a family name joined to it.

No federal agency in the United States licenses martial arts teachers or checks their ranks. A certificate from a weekend *seminar*, a short course taught by a visiting teacher, carries whatever weight the people who see it give it. Federations, registers, court rulings and the students who choose a school all take part in deciding which claims count.

words.d: the main U.S. federal trademark law, passed in 1946
the ordinary name for a whole kind of thing, which no one can own as a trademark
a short course, often over a weekend, taught by a visiting teacher
